sections.title: EFFECTIVE DAyS FOR RIDING SUSPENSIONS

nested.html: To establish the days when the suspension applies reference should be made to Chapter H.

list.html: If in the opinion of the Stewards an Interference offence warrants a suspension of more than 28 days the matter should always be referred to the Disciplinary Panel.
The level of penalty for Interference breaches should be dependent on the actual offence and previous offences should not be taken into account.
Subject to Paragraph 7, a rolling 6 month period will apply for totting up Interference suspensions, the relevant dates being the dates on which a finding of a breach was first made.
A rider should be referred to the Disciplinary Panel on the second occasion during the previous 12 months that he is found guilty of Dangerous Riding.

If a rider is found to have committed a riding offence involving Interference and it warrants a suspension and he has already been suspended from riding for a total of 20 days or more for Interference within the previous 6 months he should be referred to the Disciplinary Panel.*

After a rider has appeared before the Disciplinary Panel following a referral under Paragraphs 4 or 5 above and has been suspended, all offences prior to and including the offence for which the rider was referred are not to be taken into consideration for totting up purposes.

Suspensions imposed by the Disciplinary Panel as a result of an appeal, referral or a case instigated by the BHA are to be included in the number of days suspended during the previous 6 months. However, if the rider has already been suspended for 20 days or more the Disciplinary Panel will take this into account when imposing a penalty after which that suspension and all previous suspensions will not be taken into consideration for totting up purposes.

nested.html: * The Disciplinary Panel will usually impose a suspension of between 10 and 28 days with an entry point of 14 days for the accumulation of days suspended plus a period of suspension for the offence. Part of the suspension may be deferred for a period not exceeding 6 months but it will take effect in the event of the rider being further suspended during the said period. The said period will not commence until after the suspension from the ’totting up’ enquiry has been served. The entry point for a deferred suspension is 3 months and it is recommended that the entry point should be decreased for the ’high season’ (May to August inclusive) and increased for the ’low season’. The number of days that should be deferred are as follows:
10 - 15 days suspension 1⁄5 deferred (fractions of days will be rounded down)
16 - 25 days suspension 1⁄<sub>4 </sub>deferred
26+ days suspension 1⁄3 deferred

When a deferred suspension is activated it shall commence immediately after the conclusion of the suspension on days applicable to the rider. Suspensions that include deferred suspension days will not be subject to the Group 1/Grade 1 exception.
The deferred part of the suspension will not count towards the total number of days suspended during the current rolling 6 month period.

sections.title: PENALTY GUIDELINES

nested.html: Penalties should always reflect the effect and the cause of the interference i.e. the effect and the standard of riding. Penalties should rise as the seriousness of the interference increases.
To assist in maintaining a consistent approach to penalty the following guidelines are given for each of the three categories of Interference:

tbody.content:
Rider intentionally makes contact with another horse and/or rider resulting in serious interference.

Rider intentionally interferes with another horse and/or rider resulting in serious interference.

Rider causes serious interference as a result of steering a course or carrying out a manoeuvre when it should have been obvious to the rider that interference would result.
Rider intentionally pushes another horse and/or rider off course, including but not limited to through or around the wing of an obstacle, or through or outside the running rail
Minimal interference, due to misjudgement or inattention, which results in the sufferer having to take a slight check or horse being shifted slightly off its line.
Increased interference, due to misjudgement, inattention or failing to take corrective action, which results in the sufferer having to take a check or the horse being shifted notably off its line.

Rider allows horse to hang or drift which results in considerable interference

Rider causes considerable interference  by allowing horse to interfere with another  horse(s)  over a considerable length of time, especially  when preventing the sufferer from riding a finish.
If rider strikes or attempts to strike another horse or rider.
Rider carries out a manoeuvre and causes minimal interference - where it ought to have been obvious to the rider that interference would result
Rider carries out a manoeuvre and causes increased interference - where it ought to have been obvious to the rider that interference would result.
Rider carries out a manoeuvre and causes considerable interference - where it ought to have been obvious to the rider that interference would result.
If rider strikes or attempts to strike another horse or rider

sections.title: NOTES TO PENALTY GUIDELINES

list.html: In judging the effect, the Panel should take into consideration the overall effect on the sufferer which includes:
the degree of danger e.g. squeezed up against the rails
the loss of opportunity to challenge for prize money e.g. chance of challenging effectively destroyed
the loss of prize money e.g. sufferer comes third but would have been second but for the interference

It is important that all these aspects of the effect on the sufferer(s) are taken into account when deciding on penalty - one or other of the above ’effects’ should increase the penalty by one or even two days.
Penalty should increase when:
the horse hangs or drifts for a long period when it ought to have been obvious that, uncorrected, interference would result
the rider is coming from behind and able to assess what is in front of him
Indirect (’knock on’) interference should be taken into account when assessing the level of penalty unless you are certain that the indirect interference was not reasonably foreseeable.

When a rider is brought down the Panel should start in ‘considerable’ with an entry penalty off the bottom. Actual injuries sustained by a fallen horse or rider should not be taken into account, the fall is enough.
It is impossible to cover every eventuality and therefore the level of penalty should be varied to suit the circumstances.

sections.title: wHIPS

nested.html: A Jockey must carry an approved whip that meets the following specifications:
for a Flat Race:
the maximum length (including flap) is 70 centimetres; and
there must be no binding within 17 centimetres of the end of the flap;
for a Jump Race:
the maximum length (including flap) is 68 centimetres; and
there must be no binding within 23 centimetres of the end of the flap;
the minimum diameter for a whip is 1 centimetre;
the overall weight must not exceed 160 grams;

the contact area of the shaft must be smooth, with no protrusion or raised surface, and covered by shock absorbing material throughout its circumference such that it gives a compression factor of at least 6 millimetres;
the only additional feature that may be attached to a whip is a flap, which if attached must comply with the following requirements:
the maximum length of the flap from the end of the shaft is 10 centimetres;
the maximum width of the flap is 4 centimetres, with a minimum width of 2 centimetres;
the flap from the end of the shaft must not contain any reinforcements or additions;
the flap must have similar shock absorbing characteristics to that of the contact area
Other than adjustments to the handle or grip, a Jockey must not carry a modified whip.

nested.html: A person must make an application to the BHA in order to be registered as an Owner.
The BHA shall only register the following ownership types:
a Sole Owner;
a Company;
a Partnership;
a Syndicate; or
a Racing Club.
The BHA may refuse an application if:

any of the following are or become a Disqualified Person or subject to
any form of insolvency proceedings:
the applicant;
a director or company secretary of a company making the application;

anyone with a legal, beneficial or equitable interest in any horses
owned by the applicant; or
any representative of the applicant;
appropriate financial arrangements are not in place;
information about the applicant is not provided on request; or
it is appropriate to do so.

they do not have a horse registered with the BHA for a period of two consecutive years;

any of the following are or become a Disqualified Person or subject to

the Owner;

a director or company secretary of a
Company;

owned by the Owner; or

information is not provided on request, or is false, inaccurate or incomplete;

appropriate financial arrangements are not in place;

a participant in a Syndicate does not have any interest in a horse

sections.title: Racing colours

nested.html:
An Owner must, prior to making a Declaration to Run for a horse, register racing
colours with the Racing Calendar Office.
Registration of racing colours shall not be permitted where they are too similar to colours already registered.
The BHA may cancel the registration of racing colours if it considers it appropriate.
<u>Use of Racing Colours</u>
A horse must run in the racing colours registered by its Owner:

in Great
Britain, where the horse is trained in Great Britain, or

otherwise,
in a Recognised Racing Authority.
An Owner who has more than one set of registered racing colours must nominate which are their first colours.
Where two or more horses in a Race have similar racing colours, the BHA may require that one or more horses use alternative colours and shall determine what colours are suitable.

Where an Owner has more than one horse running in the same Race, or where the Owner’s horse shall not be carrying their first colours in a Race, the Owner or the Trainer must declare alternative colours to the Racing Calendar Office by 1pm on the day for making Declarations to Run.

The BHA may permit the joint use of racing colours if
there is sufficient connection between those who shall jointly use them.
Transfer of racing colours
The BHA shall permit a transfer of racing colours from an Owner to any of their Family Members.
The BHA may permit a transfer of racing colours from one Owner to another.

sections.title: Riding Fees And Prize Money

nested.html: GENERAL
A Jockey is not entitled to any riding fee, and the Owner is not liable for any riding fee, in respect of a Race where the Jockey is found in breach of:
Rule (F)34 (Dangerous Riding); or
Rule (G)9 (failure to present themselves to be weighed in); or
Rule (F)45 (misuse of the whip) and their horse is disqualified under Rule (L)47.11
A riding fee becomes payable:

once the signal to
mount is given, or

if permission has been given for a horse to proceed to the start early,
once the Jockey has mounted.
Where a riding fee is payable, the Owner of the horse must pay an additional sum of:
6% of the riding fee to the Trustees of the Professional Riders Insurance Scheme for application under the trusts of the Scheme; and
£4.00 into the Professional Riders Career Ending Insurance (CEI) Scheme.

An additional fee shall be payable where the Jockey has been substituted
following weighing out.
Flat Races
The riding fee payable to a Professional Jockey for a Flat Race is £173.54.

In
respect of an Apprentice Jockey, any riding fee, payable under this Fee Code, and
any Prize Money, payable to the Jockey under the Stakes and Prize Money Code,
shall be split by the Apprentice Jockey and their employer as follows:

For the avoidance of doubt, the Apprentice
Jockey shall not be entitled to claim any expenses or contributions to any
insurance premiums under the Apprentice Jockey’s Agreement with the Trainer.
Where a riding fee is payable to an Apprentice Jockey, the Apprentice Jockey must pay an additional sum of 7.2% of the fee to the BHA for the purposes of industry training.
Jump Races
The riding fee payable to a Professional Jockey for a Jump Race is £235.90.

In
respect of a Conditional Jockey, any riding fees, payable under the Fee Code,
and any Prize Money, payable to the Jockey under the Stakes and Prize Money
Code, shall be retained by the Conditional Jockey.

For
the avoidance of doubt, the Conditional Jockey shall not be entitled to claim
any expenses or contributions to any insurance premiums under the Conditional
Jockey’s Agreement with the Trainer.
Where a riding fee is payable to a Conditional Jockey, the Conditional Jockey must pay an additional sum of 5.4% of the fee to the BHA for the purposes of industry training.
Subject to paragraph 13, no fee is payable to an Amateur Jockey for a Jump Race.
Where an Amateur Jockey:
rides in a Race that is not confined solely to Amateur Jockeys;

has had more than 75 rides in Great Britain in races open to
Professional Jockeys; and
rides a horse in the Race that is not the sole property of that Amateur Jockey and/or one or more of their Family Members,

a fee is payable to the BHA for a Jump
Race of £235.90.
Physical Therapy

Where a fee is payable to a Professional Jockey, the Jockey shall pay
the additional sum of:
0.5% in respect of a Flat Race; or
0.65% in respect of a Jump Race
to the BHA for the provision of on-course physical therapy services.
Valets

A Valet shall be paid a daily attendance entitlement from the Jockeys’
Valets’ Attendance Fund in relation to each occasion that they attend and
provide services at a Race Meeting, and the rate shall be determined by the BHA.
Non-Runners

Any Professional Jockey who has been declared to ride a horse by the deadline for Declaration of Jockeys, but whose horse is subsequently made a non-runner will receive a fee of £86.77 (Flat) and £117.95 (Jump), unless;

the Professional Jockey is substituted onto another horse in the race in accordance with paragraph 64 of the Race Entry Code, whereupon the fee will be transferred to that substituted rider, provided that they were due to receive a riding fee; or
the reason for the horse being declared a non-runner was due to the Professional Jockey becoming unavailable to ride and there was no suitable replacement available.
No fee is payable where the Race Meeting or Race is abandoned or made void.
No additional payments or deductions are applicable to either fee.

The fee in paragraph 16 will not be due to any Jockey
who is declared after the deadline for Declaration of Jockeys.

Where an Amateur Jockey:

rides in a Race that is not confined solely to Amateur Jockeys; 

has had more than 75 rides in Great Britain in races open to Professional Jockeys; and

rides a horse in the Race that is not the sole property of that Amateur Jockey and/or one or more of their Family Members,

a fee is payable to the BHA for a Jump Race of £235.90.

Physical Therapy

Where a fee is payable to a Professional Jockey, the Jockey shall pay the additional sum of:

0.5% in respect of a Flat Race; or

0.65% in respect of a Jump Race

to the BHA for the provision of on-course physical therapy services.

Valets

A Valet shall be paid a daily attendance entitlement from the Jockeys’ Valets’ Attendance Fund in relation to each occasion that they attend and provide services at a Race Meeting, and the rate shall be determined by the BHA.

Non-Runners

Any Professional Jockey who has been declared to ride a horse by the deadline for Declaration of Jockeys, but whose horse is subsequently made a non-runner will receive a fee of £86.77 (Flat) and £117.95 (Jump), unless;

the Professional Jockey is substituted onto another horse in the race in accordance with paragraph 64 of the Race Entry Code, whereupon the fee will be transferred to that substituted rider, provided that they were due to receive a riding fee; or

the reason for the horse being declared a non-runner was due to the Professional Jockey becoming unavailable to ride and there was no suitable replacement available.

sections.title: GUIDANCE ON USE OF THE WHIP

nested.html: In assessing a rider’s use of the whip for referral to the Whip Review Committee the Stewards should always remember that the whip must only be used for safety and encouragement within the guidance set out below. Whilst there is a requirement for all riders to carry a whip, there is no obligation on riders using their whip.
Taking into account the below, on any occasion where the Stewards believe a rider may have committed an offence the Stewards shall refer the matter to the Whip Review Committee for consideration.
a) A rider must use an approved whip.
b) A rider may use the whip (including when waving it) in the forehand or backhand position.
c) On each occasion the whip is used when the rider’s hand is off the reins, it will count towards the permitted number of strikes.
d) A rider must not use their whip more than 6 times in a flat race or 7 times in a jump race.
e) A rider must not use their whip excessively down the shoulder in the backhand position, with their hands on the reins, for example, as an alternative to using the whip in the freehand.
f) A rider must only use the whip on the hindquarters of the horse in either the forehand or backhand position or down the shoulder with the whip in the backhand position.
g) A rider must allow 3 strides between each use of the whip.
h) A rider must only use the whip where their horse is responding.
i)	A rider must not use the whip with excessive force, for example by pulling the whip through from the opposite side of the body or rotation of the core to generate increased leverage.
j)	A rider must not use the whip with their whip arm above shoulder height, for example where there is clear space between whip hand and top of the helmet.
k)	A rider must not use the whip when out of contention, for example when there is no realistic prospect of finishing in the first five places.
l) DELETED
m)	A rider must not use the whip if their mount is clearly winning (or clearly in any other placing).
n)	A rider must not use their whip when past the winning post.
o)	A rider must not weal a horse with their whip.

sections.title: guidance for the whip review committee - RULE (F)45

nested.html: The Whip Review Committee will consider each case individually.
A breach shall be found wherever a rider has used the whip above the permitted level or has misused the whip, contrary to the guidance listed above, subject to the following exemptions.
Safety exemption:

When considering whether a rider has breached Rule (F)45 the Whip Review Committee will only exercise discretion in exceptional circumstances where individual strike(s) have been used clearly and unequivocally for safety purposes only. For example, where a horse continues to hang significantly despite the rider having visibly attempted to straighten their mount with the reins or in order to prevent a horse from running out.
corrective exemption:

When considering whether a rider has breached Rule (F)45 the Whip Review Committee may, in exceptional circumstances, exercise discretion where individual strike(s) have been used before the starting line, providing such use was reasonable, proportionate, and clearly and unequivocally for a corrective purpose only.
Where individual strikes have been found to meet either of the Exemptions, they will be discounted.

sections.title: Notes on Penalties - Rule (F)45

nested.html: Previous offences are not to be taken into account by the Whip Review Committee when deciding on the level of penalty, except when a rider has used their whip once above the permitted level, where mitigation may be applied as detailed in the penalty guidelines.

Having decided on the level of penalty the Whip Review Committee may order a Jockey to attend a course in training at the British Racing School or National Horseracing College (or other BHA directed provider) on one or more of the days suspension. When doing so the Committee should pay particular attention to where;
a) A rider uses no other method in the closing stages, to ask the horse to quicken or maintain its position, other than using the whip;
b) A rider has committed a specific misuse offence e.g. Arm above shoulder height or use of the whip in the incorrect place;
c) A rider has previously committed a breach of the same nature.

The Whip Review Committee should then establish if the rider has committed previous breaches; if it is the rider’s fourth suspension for use above the permitted level, or fifth suspension of any combination of whip offence within the previous 6 months the rider shall be referred to the Judicial Panel for penalty.
When checking previous whip offences for referral purposes, the relevant date is the date on which a finding of a breach was first made.

After a rider has appeared before the Judicial Panel following a referral under paragraph 3 and has been suspended, all offences in the 6 month period prior to and including the offence for which the rider was referred, should not be taken into account when calculating the number of subsequent offences.

If a rider is found to have committed an offence in any Class 1 race, any Class 2 race with total prize money of £150,000 or more, or any Class 2 race restricted to Apprentices, Conditionals or Amateur Jockeys only, any suspension relating to use above the permitted level shall be double that recommended in the guidance.

If a professional rider is suspended for 7 days or more (prior to any doubling of penalties in Class 1 and 2 races) they may also be fined a sum between £200 and £10,000 (£100 and £5,000 in the case of an apprentice) depending upon the type and value of the race, the rider’s finishing position and the length of the suspension imposed.

Using the same criteria in paragraph 7, amateur riders may also be fined a sum between £100 and £5000. Except, when an Amateur Jockey rides in a race that is not confined solely to Amateur Jockeys they should be fined a sum between £200 and £10,000 and treated as if a professional rider.
The amount of the fine shall be calculated by reference to that payment which the Stakes and Prize Money Code provides to be paid to the Jockey for the Race and placing in question.
If the suspension is for 7 or 8 days, the Professional Jockey shall be fined 20% of that payment, 10% in the case of an Apprentice Jockey, providing that the payment owed is £1,000 or more.
If the suspension is for 9 days or more the Professional Jockey shall be fined 40% of that payment, 20% in the case of an Apprentice Jockey, providing that the payment owed is £500 or more.

For an Amateur Jockey the amount of the fine shall be calculated by reference to that payment which the Stakes and Prize Money Code provides to be paid to a Professional Jockey for the Race and placing in question and as detailed in paragraph 9. For races solely confined to Amateur Jockeys any such fines will be calculated at the level of an Apprentice Jockey.
The Judicial Panel, when considering a referral, shall impose a suspension of between 14 days – 4 months with an entry point of 28 days.

Part of the suspension may be suspended for a period of 6 months or until the rider has ridden in 200 further flat races in Great Britain/ 150 further jump races in Great Britain, whichever is soonest, but the suspended portion will be activated in the event of the rider being further suspended for breaching Rule (F)45 during that 6 month period or before the allotted number of rides. The 6 month period/number or rides required will not commence until after the suspension for the offences has been served.
The maximum number of days of the suspension that can be deferred is 1⁄3 (fractions of days will be rounded down) up to a maximum of 9 days.

When a suspended period of suspension is activated, it will be combined with the new period of suspension to form one single sanction, made up of the appropriate new sanction, added to the activated period of suspension. For the avoidance of doubt, the provisions of Rules (H)30 and (H)31 cannot be applied in these circumstances.

nested.html: If the finding is a breach of one example, the Whip Review Committee should refer to the respective example and its corresponding penalty (as above) and then add a further 3 days for each use thereafter.

If the finding is a breach of more than one example, the Whip Review Committee should impose a single suspension to take account of all of the individual breaches. In calculating such a suspension, the Whip Review Committee should start by looking at the breach with the highest sanction and then add on further days to reflect any other breaches (including frequency). If a rider is found to have committed an offence in a race outlined at paragraph 8 of the notes on penalty any part of the suspension relating to use above the permitted level shall be double that which would be imposed in other races.
mitigation on penalty

If a rider is found to have used their whip once above the permitted level, or commits one type of misuse involving the minimum number of uses to amount to a breach (except excessive force, showing no response, or out of contention, for which mitigation cannot be applied) then the minimum penalty may be reduced dependent upon the race type and rider’s previous record. For the avoidance of doubt, where a rider is found to have used their whip once above the permitted level, and they commit another type of misuse in the same Race then mitigation will not be due.
flat race
Where a rider has had 100 or more rides in Great Britain since a previous whip offence the minimum penalty shall be reduced by 1 day to 3 days.
Where a rider has had 200 or more rides in Great Britain since a previous whip offence the minimum penalty shall be reduced by 2 days to 2 days.
jump race
Where a rider has had 75 or more rides in Great Britain since a previous whip offence the minimum penalty shall be reduced by 1 day to 3 days.
Where a rider has had 150 or more rides in Great Britain since a previous whip offence the minimum penalty shall be reduced by 2 days to 2 days.
weals
A weal shall be treated as an offence irrespective of whether any other breach has been found.Where no other breach has been found penalties shall be:
Minor Weal - 4 days
Moderate Weal - 7 days
Severe Weal - 28 days

If a rider is in breach of other aspects of Rule (F) 45 and furthermore has wealed the horse, this shall be treated as an aggravating feature, and an additional penalty will be added, and will be not less than:
Minor Weal - 7 days
Moderate Weal - 14 days
Severe Weal - 28 days

In considering whether a horse has been wealed, and whether that weal is minor, moderate or severe, the Whip Review Committee shall make a decision based upon the examination of the Veterinary Officer and the video provided.

If a rider is found to have committed an offence in a race outlined at paragraph 8 of the notes on penalty any part of the suspension relating to use above the permitted level shall be double that which would be imposed in other races.

mitigation on penalty

If a rider is found to have used their whip once above the permitted level, or commits one type of misuse involving the minimum number of uses to amount to a breach (except excessive force, showing no response, or out of contention, for which mitigation cannot be applied) then the minimum penalty may be reduced dependent upon the race type and rider’s previous record. For the avoidance of doubt, where a rider is found to have used their whip once above the permitted level, and they commit another type of misuse in the same Race then mitigation will not be due.

flat race

Where a rider has had 100 or more rides in Great Britain since a previous whip offence the minimum penalty shall be reduced by 1 day to 3 days.

Where a rider has had 200 or more rides in Great Britain since a previous whip offence the minimum penalty shall be reduced by 2 days to 2 days.

jump race

Where a rider has had 75 or more rides in Great Britain since a previous whip offence the minimum penalty shall be reduced by 1 day to 3 days.

Where a rider has had 150 or more rides in Great Britain since a previous whip offence the minimum penalty shall be reduced by 2 days to 2 days.

weals

A weal shall be treated as an offence irrespective of whether any other breach has been found.Where no other breach has been found penalties shall be:

Minor Weal - 4 days

Moderate Weal - 7 days

Severe Weal - 28 days

If a rider is in breach of other aspects of Rule (F) 45 and furthermore has wealed the horse, this shall be treated as an aggravating feature, and an additional penalty will be added, and will be not less than:

Minor Weal - 7 days

Moderate Weal - 14 days

Severe Weal - 28 days

In considering whether a horse has been wealed, and whether that weal is minor, moderate or severe, the Whip Review Committee shall make a decision based upon the examination of the Veterinary Officer and the video provided.

nested.html:
A Trainer is responsible for keeping a clear and
accurate record of any Treatment administered to each horse in their care for
at least 12 months in an Equine Medication Record Book.
Each entry in an Equine Medication Record Book must:
contain the following information:

registered name of the horse or, if it is unnamed, the
registered name of the dam and the year of foaling;
brand name or active ingredient of the Treatment used;
start and end date of the Treatment;
method of administration;

quantifiable dosage of Treatment, to include any changes to dosage
during the Treatment;

frequency of administration, to include any changes in frequency during
the Treatment; and

name of the person administering the Treatment and
whether that person is a Veterinary Surgeon.

Veterinary practice records that contain the information required for an Equine Medication Record Book entry shall be sufficient if they are available in the yard and cross-referenced in the Equine Medication Record Book.
Equine Medication Record Books must be made available for inspection when required by the BHA.

sections.title: Restrictions on a horse whilst on Racecourse Property

nested.html:
Once the Equine Welfare Integrity Officers have
commenced their duties on Racecourse Property:
a horse cannot leave Racecourse Property, unless:
to move  between the Racecourse Stables and the Racecourse; or
to go to or from any gallops which are not on Racecourse Property; or
45 minutes has elapsed since the horses Race, except where permission has been granted by a Veterinary Officer or Equine Welfare Integrity Officer.
the horse must not be stood in ice or iced water, or have a cooling device (including ice boots or bandages, or ice bags) applied to any part of the horse, unless approved by the Veterinary Officer,
until the horse has either run in the Race or been withdrawn.

9A   Once the Equine Welfare Integrity Officers have commenced their duties on Racecourse Property no equipment, save for equipment expressly permitted under the Rules of Racing, that is designed or advertised to have an effect on any mammalian body system, including but not limited to, magnetic boots, magnetic rugs, and massage pads may be used or brought onto Racecourse Property, unless approved by the Veterinary Officer.

Once the Equine Welfare and Integrity Officers have commenced their duties on Racecourse Property, no substance may be administered to a horse except for normal feed and water offered by mouth, or water administered in small quantities using a bulb syringe, unless otherwise approved by a Veterinary Officer.

Any medical treatment given to a horse on Racecourse Property must first be authorised by the Veterinary Officer, except where a horse needs to be humanely euthanised and it is not possible to consult the Veterinary Officer first.

sections.title: General

nested.html:
A Jockey must weigh out for each Race in which they
are declared to ride, except that they shall not be permitted to do so if they
are 4lbs or more over weight.
An Amateur Jockey must present their Medical Record Book if requested by a Racecourse Medical Officer or an Official.
Weighing out must be completed 15 minutes before the start of the Race.
A Jockey must:

weigh out wearing the correct colours, and present their colours cap and number cloth to the Clerk of the
Scales; and

place on the scales all equipment to be worn or carried in the Race,
except for Excluded Equipment.
All weights shall be rounded down to the nearest 1lb unit.
Jockeys will be given a 4lb safety allowance.
After weighing out for a Race both the Jockey and the Trainer are responsible for ensuring that:

the Jockey’s saddle is not left unattended or taken back into the
Jockey’s changing room;
the clothing and equipment a Jockey wore when weighing out is not changed except that the girth or surcingle can be changed if they do not fit;

the Jockey does not accept anything from, or give
anything to, another person which may affect the Jockey’s weight; and
no lead is added to or removed from the Jockey’s weight cloth.
A Jockey must ride the horse for which they have been weighed out.
The Trainer, or representative of the Trainer, of a horse to be ridden by an Apprentice Jockey or Conditional Jockey must be present when the Apprentice Jockey or Conditional Jockey is weighed out.

nested.html: GUIDANCE NOTE

Save in circumstances where a ‘Solution’ or ‘Fast-Track’ is considered appropriate the breach will be referred to the Disciplinary Panel for a decision on whether a breach has occurred and, if it has, what the appropriate penalty is.

This guidance should not be seen as either a replacement for, or an interpretation of, the Rules of Racing. The guidelines as to penalties are not intended to override the discretion of the Disciplinary Panel. However, in the interest of consistency and fairness, Panels are expected to operate within the guidelines unless they have good reason to consider that there are exceptional circumstances in the case before them which justifies a greater or lesser penalty outside the guidelines; Panels should be prepared to explain their reasons for so doing.
When considering what penalty would be appropriate for a breach that is proven, a Disciplinary Panel will first decide how serious the breach is and whether it is a low, medium or high level breach.

Once that assessment has been made, the tables below set out the recommended penalty for low, medium and high-level breaches. Panels should start at the entry point for the appropriate level of breach, as identified by the Panel, and adjust for the mitigating and aggravating features they have found as part of their consideration of the evidence.

A financial penalty only should be imposed in exceptional circumstances only. The exceptional circumstances must be identified and explained by the Disciplinary Panel. The Disciplinary Panel will need to consider carefully the impact of suspension/withdrawal/disqualification or exclusion on individuals who rely on the sport as their primary source of income. In suitable cases, it may be proportionate to suspend part of or all of the sanction dependent upon future compliance with the Code and the successful completion of appropriate training courses.
STAGE 1

The Disciplinary Panel must first assess the level of culpability. The below <u>may</u> form part of the considerations of the Disciplinary Panel but the Panel will form their own view of the evidence and all factors relevant to the assessment of culpability.

tbody.content:
- A single breach of the Code and the Person has engaged appropriately in the Disciplinary Process. 
- Limited or no harm caused to the victim and/or impact upon the reputation of the sport.
- No or limited previous disciplinary history.

- A single breach involving harm to the victim and/or impact upon the reputation of the sport. 
- Persistent less serious breaches of the code. 
- Evidence of premeditation or a pattern of misconduct. 
- Limited or no engagement with the Disciplinary Process.

- Serious harm caused to the victim and/or impact upon the reputation of the sport. 
- Limited or no engagement with the Disciplinary Process. 
- Misconduct involving discrimination based on protected characteristics or a vulnerable victim.
- Sexual misconduct.- Criminal conduct. 
- Manipulation of or attempts to interfere with witnesses and victims.

nested.html: STAGE 2
Once an Assessment of Culpability has been made the Penalty Guidance is as follows.

sections.title: Welfare

nested.html: (D)1 - Horse welfare

British horseracing prides itself on demanding and ensuring that racehorses receive the best possible lifetime care. This is our moral and ethical duty to the racehorse. Achieving anything less than this is a major reputational risk to the sport and, more importantly, a risk to the racehorses our sport relies upon. The standard of care expected of a Responsible Person, tasked with ensuring the safety and welfare of horses in their care having sought and accepted that responsibility through the BHA Licensing process, is a high one.
Stage 1 - culpability

The Disciplinary Panel must assess the level of culpability of the Responsible Person by weighing up all the factors of the case. Where there are characteristics present which fall under different levels of culpability the Panel should balance these characteristics to reach a fair assessment. Culpability is demonstrated by one of more of the following (non-exhaustive):
ASSESSMENT OF CULPABILITY
Low:

list.html: Behaviour that falls below the standard expected of a Responsible Person
Single incident of very short duration

nested.html: Medium:

list.html: Behaviour that falls far below the standard expected of a Responsible Person
Behaviour that falls below the standard expected of a Responsible Person and occurs over a period of time, including but not limited to, unreasonable delays in seeking appropriate veterinary advice
Neglect
Very poor husbandry

nested.html: High:

list.html: Cruelty
Behaviour deliberately intended to cause significant harm
Prolonged and/or repeated incidents or behaviour that might otherwise fall into medium level culpability.

nested.html: stage 2 - harm

The Disciplinary Panel must then assess the harm that has been caused to the horse(s). Where there are characteristics present which fall under different levels of harm the Panel should balance these characteristics to reach a fair assessment.
Harm is demonstrated by one or more of the following (non-exhaustive):
Category 1:

list.html: No/little physical or developmental harm/suffering/distress to the horse(s)
No ongoing/long-lasting issues/effects

nested.html: Category 2:

list.html: Moderate physical or developmental harm/suffering/distress caused to the horse(s)
Ongoing/long-lasting issues/effects

nested.html: Category 3:

list.html: Very high level of physical or developmental harm/suffering/distress caused to the horse(s)
Death (including injury/condition necessitating euthanasia)

nested.html: NOTE: Where there was a real risk of more serious harm or long-lasting issues being caused to the horses(s) than actually resulted, the Panel should give serious consideration to an increase in categorisation.
stage 3 - starting point and range

Once the Panel has decided upon the levels of culpability and harm, they will then decide upon sanction. Each case should be considered on the basis of its factual circumstances and previous precedent is unlikely to be considered relevant. Panels should start at the Entry Point and adjust for the mitigating and aggravating features they have found as part of their consideration of the evidence. At this stage the Panel can take into consideration further mitigating or aggravating features such as the Responsible Person’s personal mitigation, credit for cooperation with the BHA (if considered appropriate) or their previous history of disciplinary offences. This might necessitate a shift, either upwards or downwards within the range provided.

British horseracing prides itself on demanding and ensuring that racehorses receive the best possible lifetime care. This is our moral and ethical duty to the racehorse. Achieving anything less than this is a major reputational risk to the sport and, more importantly, a risk to the racehorses our sport relies upon. The standard of care expected of a Responsible Person, tasked with ensuring the safety and welfare of horses in their care having sought and accepted that responsibility through the BHA Licensing process, is a high one.

Stage 1 - culpability

The Disciplinary Panel must assess the level of culpability of the Responsible Person by weighing up all the factors of the case. Where there are characteristics present which fall under different levels of culpability the Panel should balance these characteristics to reach a fair assessment. Culpability is demonstrated by one of more of the following (non-exhaustive):

ASSESSMENT OF CULPABILITY

Low:

  • Behaviour that falls below the standard expected of a Responsible Person
  • Single incident of very short duration

Medium:

  • Behaviour that falls far below the standard expected of a Responsible Person
  • Behaviour that falls below the standard expected of a Responsible Person and occurs over a period of time, including but not limited to, unreasonable delays in seeking appropriate veterinary advice
  • Neglect
  • Very poor husbandry

High:

  • Cruelty
  • Behaviour deliberately intended to cause significant harm
  • Prolonged and/or repeated incidents or behaviour that might otherwise fall into medium level culpability.

stage 2 - harm

The Disciplinary Panel must then assess the harm that has been caused to the horse(s). Where there are characteristics present which fall under different levels of harm the Panel should balance these characteristics to reach a fair assessment.

Harm is demonstrated by one or more of the following (non-exhaustive):

Category 1:

  • No/little physical or developmental harm/suffering/distress to the horse(s)
  • No ongoing/long-lasting issues/effects

Category 2:

  • Moderate physical or developmental harm/suffering/distress caused to the horse(s)
  • Ongoing/long-lasting issues/effects

Category 3:

  • Very high level of physical or developmental harm/suffering/distress caused to the horse(s)
  • Death (including injury/condition necessitating euthanasia)

NOTE: Where there was a real risk of more serious harm or long-lasting issues being caused to the horses(s) than actually resulted, the Panel should give serious consideration to an increase in categorisation.

stage 3 - starting point and range

Once the Panel has decided upon the levels of culpability and harm, they will then decide upon sanction. Each case should be considered on the basis of its factual circumstances and previous precedent is unlikely to be considered relevant. Panels should start at the Entry Point and adjust for the mitigating and aggravating features they have found as part of their consideration of the evidence. At this stage the Panel can take into consideration further mitigating or aggravating features such as the Responsible Person’s personal mitigation, credit for cooperation with the BHA (if considered appropriate) or their previous history of disciplinary offences. This might necessitate a shift, either upwards or downwards within the range provided.

sections.title: Rule (K)2.1 – Category A – Prohibited At All Times

nested.html: STAGE 1

The Disciplinary Panel must assess the level of culpability of the Responsible Person by reference solely to the facts that have been established (if any) relating to the source, the involvement of the Responsible Person and the precautions in place at the yard.

tbody.content: No knowledge of administration and reasonable precautions taken. Satisfactory attendance at BHA/NTF Seminars is a required precaution.
No knowledge of administration but significant failings at the yard or Panel is satisfied of an acceptable explanation for an administration error.
Deliberate administration or serious failings in the administration of the yard bordering upon negligence.

nested.html: STAGE 2

Once the Panel has decided upon the level of culpability, they will then decide upon sanction. Each case should be considered on the basis of its factual circumstances and previous precedent ought not normally be considered. Panels should start at the Entry Point and adjust for the mitigating and aggravating features that they have found as part of their consideration of the evidence and during their assessment of the level of culpability. At this stage the Panel can take into consideration further mitigating or aggravating features such as the Responsible Person’s personal mitigation, credit for cooperation with the BHA or their previous history of disciplinary offences. This might necessitate a shift, either upwards or downwards in the assessment of the level of culpability.

tbody.content: 2 years suspension*/disqualification suspended for 24 months & financial penalty of £1,000.

2 years disqualification**
(If suspended – Financial Penalty of £2,000)

nested.html: * Suspension can only be considered for Category A substances captured by paragraph 6 of the prohibited list code. All other Category A substances must be dealt with by way of a period of disqualification.
**Disqualification can be suspended for a 24 month period.
GUIDANCE NOTE

The Panel must impose a financial penalty in addition to any suspended period of disqualification. No suspended penalty can be imposed for a High level breach. There is no alternative financial penalty available at any level. Any Disciplinary Panel considering any further breach of the Rules of Racing may activate the suspended penalty if the Panel considers it appropriate in the circumstances.

General

nested.html:
<u>Selection of Disciplinary
Panel and Appeal Board members</u>
The Judicial Panel Chairman shall select members of:

a Disciplinary Panel or Licensing Committee from the Disciplinary and Licensing Panel Pool, one of whom shall be selected as chairperson, in accordance with the Disciplinary Panel Terms of Reference or the Licensing Committee Terms of Reference; and
an Appeal Board from the Appeal Board Pool, one of whom shall be selected as chairperson, in accordance with the Appeal Board Terms of Reference.
Each member of a Disciplinary Panel, Licensing Committee or Appeal Board must declare if they have a conflict or an interest in a case. If they do, they must either:
recuse themselves; or
obtain the consent of the parties to stay on the Disciplinary Panel, Licensing Committee or Appeal Board (as applicable).

Where a conflict or an interest in a case is declared, and the member neither recuses themselves in accordance with paragraph 2.1, nor obtains the consent of the parties in accordance with paragraph 2.2;
the Disciplinary Panel Chairperson, Licensing Committee Chairperson or Appeal Board Chairperson (as applicable) shall determine whether the panel member shall remain on the panel; or

where the panel member in question is the Disciplinary Panel Chairperson, Licensing Committee Chairperson or Appeal Board Chairperson (as applicable), the Judicial Panel Chairperson shall decide whether the panel member shall remain on the panel.

sections.title: General

nested.html: Paragraphs 5 to 32 shall be referred to as the Procedural Rules. The Procedural Rules shall cover:
Disciplinary Panels as a first instance body;
Disciplinary Panels as an appellate body; and
Appeal Boards

Judicial Panels shall have the power to regulate their own procedure. The chairperson of the panel will normally determine procedural matters alone and, where submissions from the parties are required, such submissions will normally be requested in writing and without a hearing.

Any breach of procedure by a Judicial Panel, or a failure by them to follow any direction given (including any time limit), shall not invalidate the proceedings or its outcome unless the breach is such as to seriously and irredeemably prejudice the position of the parties.

Judicial Panels are disciplinary, rather than arbitral, bodies. In the interests of achieving a just and fair result, procedural and technical considerations must take second place to the paramount object of being just and fair to all parties.

Judicial Panels shall have the power, where the subject matter or facts are sufficiently linked and where appropriate for the efficient disposal of proceedings, to consolidate proceedings so that they are conducted together and determined at a joint hearing. The circumstances in which the power may be exercised include:
where breaches are alleged to have been committed in the same Race or at the same meeting; or
where there is common evidence.
The chairperson of the panel will give such directions as they consider appropriate for the fair and expeditious conduct of the case to include, but not limited to:
lengthening or shortening any time limit;
adapting or dispensing with any procedural steps; and
holding a preliminary hearing.
A party may apply to the Judicial Panel Chairman where it wishes to have a preliminary matter determined by a separate Judicial Panel.

Judicial Panels shall have the power to regulate their own procedure. The chairperson of the panel will normally determine procedural matters alone and, where submissions from the parties are required, such submissions will normally be requested in writing and without a hearing.

Any breach of procedure by a Judicial Panel, or a failure by them to follow any direction given (including any time limit), shall not invalidate the proceedings or its outcome unless the breach is such as to seriously and irredeemably prejudice the position of the parties.

Judicial Panels are disciplinary, rather than arbitral, bodies. In the interests of achieving a just and fair result, procedural and technical considerations must take second place to the paramount object of being just and fair to all parties.

Judicial Panels shall have the power, where the subject matter or facts are sufficiently linked and where appropriate for the efficient disposal of proceedings, to consolidate proceedings so that they are conducted together and determined at a joint hearing. The circumstances in which the power may be exercised include:

where breaches are alleged to have been committed in the same Race or at the same meeting; or

where there is common evidence.

The chairperson of the panel will give such directions as they consider appropriate for the fair and expeditious conduct of the case to include, but not limited to:

lengthening or shortening any time limit;

adapting or dispensing with any procedural steps; and

holding a preliminary hearing.

A party may apply to the Judicial Panel Chairman where it wishes to have a preliminary matter determined by a separate Judicial Panel.

sections.title: Charge Response Form

nested.html: Each Respondent must complete the Charge Response Form by stating:
whether they admit or deny each alleged breach;
their response to the evidence against them, irrespective of whether they admit or deny the charges;
where the breaches are admitted, any representations on sanction;
the name of any witness they intend to call to give oral evidence at the hearing, together with a witness statement or summary of the witness’ proposed oral evidence; and

where they deny each alleged breach or make partial admissions, and where the BHA relies on witness evidence, any witnesses they want to question at the hearing (for the avoidance of doubt, where a Respondent does not notify of a wish to question a witness called by the BHA, that witness’ evidence shall be deemed to be accepted).

The Charge Response Form must be accompanied by copies of all evidence, documents and written submissions upon which the Respondent intends to rely unless the BHA agrees to an extension of time to the period stated on the form.

The Charge Response Form must be served on the BHA within the period stated on the form, unless the BHA agrees to an extension of time or such other time as the Disciplinary Panel chairperson orders..
If a Respondent introduces evidence late, the Disciplinary Panel may:
allow or refuse the admission of that evidence; or
adjourn a hearing.
Where a hearing is adjourned in accordance with paragraph 38.2 the Disciplinary Panel may make an order for costs against the Respondent.
The BHA may offer the Respondent the opportunity to enter into the fast track process in accordance with the Fast Track Protocol.

Upon review of the Charge Response Form and the accompanying materials, the BHA may provide the Respondent with any further evidence or material on which it intends to rely. The Respondent will be given an opportunity to respond to that evidence or material.
The Disciplinary Panel may make an interim decision affecting a penalty or award, order or other sanction.

sections.title: Plea agreements

nested.html: The BHA and the Respondent may attempt to agree:
that the Respondent admits a charge in return for a reduced sanction;
that the Respondent admits one or more charges in return for others not being pursued by the BHA; and / or
some or all of the facts relating to the charge,(a Plea Agreement).
(a Plea Agreement).
If a Plea Agreement is sought by the Respondent, they should request discussions at an early stage.
A Plea Agreement is always subject to the approval of the Disciplinary Panel so it can assess whether the agreement:
accurately and appropriately reflects the available evidence; and
is fair and in the interests of justice.
If a Plea Agreement is agreed the Disciplinary Panel must be provided with:
full details of the Plea Agreement; and
the facts of the case which should, where possible, be agreed.
If agreement is reached on certain issues, but not others, the BHA and the Respondent may agree to seek directions from the Disciplinary Panel as to how to proceed.

The Disciplinary Panel will not be informed of discussions if they do not result in agreement. However, the Disciplinary Panel and any other party to the proceedings may be informed of any relevant documents or information referred to during those discussions that is not already before the Disciplinary Panel, including any admissions made.

where appropriate, apply for leave to present new evidence pursuant to paragraphs 86 to 88.
If the decision being appealed against relates to a breach of Rule (F)37:

the Appellant must lodge a Notice of Appeal within 48 hours of service of the full written reasons which complies with paragraph 76.1 and, in respect of an appeal brought by any person other than the BHA, with paragraph 78.2; and
the Appellant must then, within 7 days of service of the full written reasons, comply with paragraphs 78.3 to 78.4.
The Notice of Appeal must be accompanied by copies of all evidence, documents and written submissions upon which the Appellant intends to rely.
If a person appeals a decision of a Disciplinary Panel, the BHA will provide a transcript of the Disciplinary Panel hearing to the person as soon as practicable.
<u>Relief from lodging deposit</u>
An Appellant seeking relief from the requirement to lodge a deposit on the sole ground of hardship must, at the same time as the Notice of Appeal, lodge an application which:
requests relief from the deposit requirement; and
sets out the relevant grounds and facts supporting the claim of hardship.

The request for relief shall be considered by the chairperson of the Appeal Board, whose decision whether to grant total, partial or no relief shall be final and without any requirement to give reasons.
Convening an Appeal Board and procedure
Upon receipt of a valid Notice of Appeal, the Judicial Panel Chairman shall convene an Appeal Board.

The chairperson of the Appeal Board may, whether upon the application of a party or of their own motion, give any instructions considered necessary for the proper conduct of the proceedings including, but not limited to:
setting a timetable and issuing directions as required for the conduct of the appeal; and
requiring a Disciplinary Panel to clarify and/or amplify some aspect of the reasons given for the decision.
<u>New evidence</u>
No new evidence shall be permitted, except where the Appeal Board directs otherwise.

An application for permission to admit new evidence must be made in the Notice of Appeal or in any response, setting out the nature and the relevance of the new evidence and why it was not introduced at the original hearing.
The Appeal Board shall grant permission if:
it is satisfied as to why the evidence was not, or could not reasonably have been, introduced at the original hearing; or
there are other exceptional circumstances.
<u>Appeal Board proceedings</u>
An appeal shall be by way of review of materials considered at the original hearing, except that:
oral submissions will be permitted; and
oral evidence will only be permitted if permission to introduce new evidence has been granted.
An Appeal Board may in exceptional circumstances order that the appeal takes place as a full rehearing of the case.

Where a party fails to comply with an order, requirement or instruction of the Appeal Board, The Appeal Board may, take any action it considers appropriate, including taking that conduct into account when determining costs.
Decision
After hearing an appeal, an Appeal Board shall have the power to:
allow or dismiss the appeal;
exercise any power which the original decision maker could have exercised, including increasing or decreasing any penalty, award, order or other sanction;
remit the matter for re-hearing;
make a costs award, to include the forfeit of any deposit, in accordance with paragraphs 99 to 102; and/or
make such further or other order as it considers appropriate, either generally or for the purpose of giving effect to its decision.
Any decision of the Appeal Board or Appeal Board Chairperson, including procedural decisions, shall be final and binding.
If an Appeal Board is unable to reach a decision, the Appeal Board Chairperson shall convene a new Appeal Board.
As soon as practicable after the hearing, the Appeal Board shall publish a written statement of its decision, stating:
the name of the Appellant, the decision(s) appealed against and the grounds of appeal;
the outcome of the appeal;

the date on which any penalty will be effective, if it
is not the day after the date on which the appeal is finally determined; and
the order(s) made by the Appeal Board.

Where requested to by a party to the appeal within 5 days of announcement of the decision, the Appeal Board shall within a reasonable timeframe give written reasons for the decision. The written reasons may be published in such manner as the Appeal Board Chairperson considers appropriate.
A decision of an Appeal Board to:
withdraw or suspend a Licence for a period of 3 months or more; or
declare a Person to be a Disqualified Person,

shall take effect immediately on the announcement of the decision
unless the BHA or a Judicial Panel directs otherwise.
Any decision not covered by paragraph 97 shall become effective:
after the time for bringing an appeal has expired, or

if an appeal is brought, the day after the date on
which the appeal:
is finally determined by an Appeal Board;
is abandoned; or
fails by reason of non-prosecution,
unless the Appeal Board directs otherwise.

sections.title: Costs and deposit

nested.html: Subject to paragraphs 100 and 101, an Appeal Board shall have the power to make such order as to costs, in respect of those incurred both in relation to the first instance hearing and the appeal, as it considers appropriate.

Subject to paragraph 101, where the BHA brings an appeal which fails, the Appeal Board shall order that the BHA shall pay the respondent’s costs of the appeal except to the extent the Appeal Board determines that:
the Respondent has acted unreasonably in connection with the appeal; or
the costs incurred by the Respondent in connection with the appeal are unreasonable.
An Appeal Board may not issue a costs order in excess of £20,000.
A deposit may be returned, except:

that it shall be forfeited where the Appeal Board
concludes that the appeal had no realistic prospect of success. In such
circumstances, the written reasons shall address the issue; or

where the Appeal Board orders it to be applied towards the satisfaction
of any costs award.

sections.title: PERMISSION FOR APPEAL

nested.html:
A person seeking to appeal a decision of the BHA in
relation to a Licence must first seek permission from the
Licensing Committee. The request for permission must be made within 21 days of
receipt of the decision being challenged and must include:

reasons why the decision being challenged should have
been different, together with any supporting documentation;

if sought, the reasons why the request for permission should be heard
at an oral hearing; and
the name and contact details of any legal representative.
The Licensing Committee may request that further evidence is submitted before determining whether they will give permission for an appeal.
The Licensing Committee will:
only hold a hearing if one is required;

grant permission to proceed with an appeal if the Licence applicant can
demonstrate that:
the appeal has a real prospect of success; or
there is some other compelling reason why the appeal should be heard; and
give written reasons for its decision.
If the Licensing Committee does not give permission, the Licence applicant has no further rights of appeal.
If the Licensing Committee does give permission, it shall consider the Licence application on a de novo basis.

sections.title: CONDUCT OF LICENSING COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS

nested.html:
The Licensing Committee shall set directions for the fair and
expeditious determination of a matter:
on receipt of a referral from the BHA;
if permission to proceed with an appeal is granted; or
if a matter is referred to them pursuant to Rule (B)24.
If necessary, the Licensing Committee may request that any person:
produce any relevant documents; and / or
attend any hearing to answer questions.
The Licence applicant or their legal representative must attend the hearing.
The Licence applicant shall be given sufficient opportunity to:
make representations and call witnesses on any matter relevant to the hearing;

provide further information with respect to any matter
on which the Licensing Committee has sought clarification;

ask relevant questions of anyone appearing before the Licensing
Committee; and
address the Licensing Committee.
If any person required to attend the hearing fails to do so, the Licensing Committee may:
adjourn the hearing;
proceed with the hearing in their absence; or

in the case of an appeal, dismiss the application in which case the
original decision of the BHA will
stand.

A Licensing Committee hearing shall be inquisitorial
and cross-examination shall not be permitted, unless the Licensing Committee
considers it is required for the fair determination of the hearing.

sections.title: Getting to the start

nested.html: Trainers and Jockeys must ensure that their horses are ready to start on time.
Horses must be ridden to the start.
Horses may not be led on the course on the way to the start, except:
when in a Parade; or
with the prior permission of the Stewards.
Jockeys are not permitted to jump a fence or hurdle before the start of a Race.
If a Jockey remounts after leaving the parade ring they must:
be assessed by a Racecourse Medical Officer or ambulance paramedic; or
inform the Starter that they remounted,
before riding in the Race.

sections.title: False starts

nested.html: The signal for a false start is the waving of the Starting Flag.
A Starter shall declare a false start:

if any faulty action of the starting gate or starting stalls has meant
that there has not been a fair start;
when a horse has broken away before the Race has been declared ‘Off’;

if the Starter releases the starting gate or starting stalls for safety reasons but does
not intend to start the Race; or
if the recall procedures have been initiated.
Where a false start has been declared the Jockeys must return to the start.
A horse shall be withdrawn if, following a false start and before the Race has restarted:
in a Flat Race, it completes the course; or

in a Jump Race, it either completes a circuit of the
course, unseats its Jockey other than at the start, or falls.

sections.title: Stalls Tests

nested.html: All Persons must comply with the Stalls Test Code.

Any horse reported by a Starter for a Stalls Test cannot run in a Race started from starting stalls until the day after it has passed a Stalls Test, or gained an equivalent certificate from a Recognised Racing Authority.
A Starter may report a horse for a Stalls Test if the horse:
failed to enter the starting stalls;
unnecessarily delayed the start; or
was unruly.
A Starter may give a Trainer a warning in respect of a horse if:
the horse was unruly; or
a Late Load Request was requested for the horse.

Subject to paragraph 18.2 below, Late Load Request(s) are restricted to horses that have had a demonstrative behaviour reason inside of the starting stalls as identified in a previous race in Great Britain.
A horse having its debut run will be ineligible for a Late Load Request unless it has undertaken a pre-race assessment showing a demonstrative behaviour concern inside of the starting stalls.
If a Trainer is given three warnings in respect of the same horse within a 12 month period, the horse must complete a Stalls Test.

Where a horse has completed a Stalls Tests as a
result of behaviour inside the starting stalls, any further Late Load Request(s) for that horse will not result in additional warnings for a 12-month period commencing from the date of the Starters Report

Where a horse is subject to a third Starter’s report, it may not
attempt a Stalls Test for six months.

sections.title: Pulling up a horse

nested.html: A Jockey must pull up their horse whenever:
it is lame or injured;
it has no more to give or has tailed off through fatigue; or
has a problem which is materially affecting its performance.

they cannot re-join the Race or jump any further fence or hurdle; and
they must wait in the area where they pulled up until all horses still in the Race have passed.

sections.title: Procedure for division

nested.html:
If a Weight-for-Age Race divides, the following shall be allocated to
different divisions where possible:
horses owned by the same Owner;
horses trained by the same Trainer;

horses that have won a Race of the same type as
the dividing Race on or after 1 January of the previous year; and
horses set to carry the same colours.
If a Handicap Race divides:

horses shall be ordered by weight and allocated to alternating
divisions; and
thereafter, the following shall be allocated to different divisions where possible:
horses owned by the same Owner;
horses trained by the same Trainer; and
horses set to carry the same colours.

sections.title: General

nested.html: The order of elimination shall be determined in accordance with this Race Administration Code. Where the order of elimination cannot be determined in accordance with those paragraphs, random balloting shall be conducted to determine the order of elimination for horses.
Horses with the same weight and allocated a Handicap Rating of 45 or below shall be eliminated in order from the lowest to the highest Handicap Rating.

Any horse previously omitted from a Handicap Race, or given an incorrect weight, shall be added randomly to any horses on the same weight and such horse shall be subject to elimination, if necessary, in accordance with that revised random order.

All penalties shall be added to a horse’s Handicap Rating to determine the order of elimination, except for any penalty that causes a horse that was within the Rating Range at Closing to subsequently exceed the Upper Rating Limit.

Unless otherwise specified, the Handicap Rating used for elimination shall be based on Races run up to and including the Saturday before Closing or, where the Race is an Early Closer, the Saturday before Confirmation of Entries.

Where a horse does not have a relevant Handicap Rating, it shall instead be assessed by the Handicapper based on Races run up to and including the Saturday before Closing or, where the Race is an Early Closer, the Saturday before Confirmation of Entries.
The Handicapper may decline to allot a rating or give an assessment of a horse if they do not have sufficient information to make a decision.
If a horse is eliminated by mistake;
the BHA may correct the elimination; but
no correction shall be made after 2pm on the day before the Race.

sections.title: Order of elimination

nested.html: <u>Handicap Races</u>

The order of elimination shall be determined in accordance with paragraphs 19 to 23 below. These elimination provisions shall not apply to horses that are protected from elimination in accordance with paragraphs 24 to 44.
Elimination shall occur in Handicap Races, except for Races specified in paragraphs 20 to 23, in the following order:
horses rated 2lb or more above the Upper Rating Limit;
horses rated 1lb or more above the Upper Rating Limit;
horses with the lowest weights in order of lowest weight first; and
where it is necessary to eliminate some horses with the same weights:
first, that have incurred penalties in order of highest penalty; and
second, that have not incurred penalties.
Grand National Steeple Chase
Elimination shall occur in the Grand National Steeple Chase in the following order:
horses with the lowest weights; and

where it is necessary to eliminate some horses with
the same weights, in order of lowest Handicap Rating at the time of elimination.
Pattern Races, Listed Races and Conditions Stakes Races except for Handicap Races
Elimination shall occur in Pattern Races, Listed Races and Conditions Stakes Races, other than Handicap Races, in the following order:
horses that have not run shall be eliminated by random ballot;

horses with the lowest Handicap Rating or, in the case of any horse that does not qualify for a Handicap Rating, lowest assessment by the Handicapper once the following have been taken into consideration;
Any such penalty that is due to be carried shall be deducted from the Handicap Rating to determine the rating used for the purpose of elimination
Any sex allowance due in accordance with Paragraph 49 of the Weights and Handicapping Code shall be added to the Handicap Rating to determine the rating used for the purpose of elimination.

For the purposes of paragraph 21.2, Trainers of horses previously trained outside Great Britain and Ireland are advised to notify the Handicapper five days in advance of submitting an Entry in order for performances outside Great Britain and Ireland to be assessed. Failure to do so may result in such horses being eliminated first by random ballot. The Handicapper's decision to allot a rating or give an assessment when the above notification has not been fulfilled shall be final.
Classified Stakes Races, Rating Related Maiden Races and classified Claiming Races
Elimination shall occur in Classified Stakes Races, Rating Related Maiden Races and classified Claiming Races in order of lowest Handicap Rating.

nested.html: Horses that would be eliminated from a Race in accordance with paragraphs 10 to 23 may be eligible for protection from elimination in accordance with paragraphs 25 to 44 below.

Races run shall include:

for Early Closers, Races up to and including the Saturday
before Confirmations of Entry are due; and

for Races that are not Early
Closers, Races up to and including the Saturday before Closing.
if two or more horses:

have the same highest placing, priority shall be given to the
horse with the greatest number of finishes at that placing followed by the greatest
number of finishes at the next highest placing; and

cannot be distinguished using any of the specified
eligibility criteria, priority shall be determined by random ballot.
Flat Races
Protection from elimination shall operate for Flat Races, other than those listed in paragraph 28, in the following order of priority, subject to paragraph 27:

horses that have not run in a
Flat Race;

horses that have run in or
completed no more than two Flat Races;

horses that have the highest

horses with the fewest

Classified Stakes Races;

Rating Related Maiden Races;

Classified Claiming Races; and

Flat Novice Races and Maiden Races.

Flat Novice and Maiden Races Races

Protection from elimination in Flat Novice Races and non-Rating Related Maiden Races shall operate as follows, subject to paragraph 30:

horses that have run in or completed no more than two Flat Races and have been placed in the first four at least once in those Races;

horses that have not run in a Flat Race;

horses that have run in or completed no more than one Flat Race;
